tasks.title: Build a deterministic, versioned cache key
tasks.description: Implement cache_key(string $resource, int $version, array $parts): string — a deterministic, namespaced, versioned cache-key builder. Every key must start with the 'cache:' namespace, contain the resource name, embed the version as ':v{N}', then append each part separated by ':'. Parts must be appended in sorted order so that the same set of parts always yields the same key regardless of the order they are passed in (deterministic). Examples: cache_key('articles', 2, ['42', 'en']) === 'cache:articles:v2:42:en'; cache_key('articles', 2, ['en', '42']) === 'cache:articles:v2:42:en' (same key — order-independent); cache_key('articles', 3, ['en', '42']) === 'cache:articles:v3:42:en'; cache_key('users', 1, []) === 'cache:users:v1'.

tasks.title: Fix the inverted cache-stampede guard
tasks.description: should_recompute(bool $cacheHit, bool $holdsLock): bool is the decision core of a cache-stampede guard on a hot read path. Correct contract: it must return true ONLY when the cache MISSED and THIS request holds the recompute lock (it is the single winner that rebuilds the cache). A cache HIT must never trigger a recompute, and a request that lost the lock race must NOT recompute — it should wait briefly and re-read the cache, which the lock owner has just repopulated. Bug hint: the boolean logic is inverted — trace when the current code returns true on a hit and when it returns true without holding the lock; those are exactly the branches that cause wasted queries and a stampede of simultaneous recomputes into the database.

tasks.title: Design caching for a hot, read-mostly product endpoint
tasks.description: Your Laravel service exposes a product-details endpoint that is read thousands of times per second, while the underlying MySQL product data changes only a few times a day. Users report latency spikes during traffic peaks. Design a caching strategy and defend your choices: (1) pick a pattern — cache-aside vs write-through/read-through — and justify it for this read-heavy, write-light profile; (2) define the TTL policy and the write path (explicit invalidation and key versioning); (3) protect the endpoint from a cache stampede when a hot key expires, using Redis locks such as Cache::lock; (4) handle cache penetration (lookups for rows that do not exist), hot-key breakdown, and avalanche of many keys expiring at once; (5) state clearly when you would NOT cache a resource.
tasks.solution:
Start with **cache-aside** (lazy loading): read `Cache::get($key)`; on a miss, query MySQL, store the result under a versioned key with a TTL, and return it. Cache-aside fits this workload because reads dwarf writes and it avoids the write-path cost of write-through, which pays write latency to store values users may never read. Writes are rare, so make them explicit: on every product update call `Cache::forget($key)` — or better, embed a per-resource version in each key (`products:v3`) and bump it once, invalidating the whole class of keys in a single operation.

A TTL is a safety net, not the correctness mechanism: pick a short-but-useful TTL (5–10 minutes for product data), rely on explicit invalidation for freshness, and add random jitter per key so related keys never expire in lock-step.

**Cache stampede**: when the hot key expires at peak load, thousands of requests would all hit MySQL at once. Acquire an atomic lock — `Cache::lock($key, 10)->get()` — the winner recomputes and repopulates the cache while the losers `block()` briefly and then re-read, finding the fresh value. If the lock cannot be obtained in time, fall back to stale-while-revalidate: serve the previous value and refresh in the background.

**Penetration / breakdown / avalanche**: cache short-lived negative results (or keep a bloom filter) so requests for absent ids never reach the store; never let the single hottest key expire cold — warm it proactively just before its TTL; spread expiries with jitter so thousands of keys do not vanish in the same second.

**When NOT to cache**: per-user secrets, data already living in Redis (sessions, queues), values rewritten on nearly every request, and anything where even a few seconds of staleness is unacceptable (balances, counters, idempotency). Every cache is a disposable failure point: the source of truth must always be rebuildable, and you should monitor the hit ratio and alert on drops.

criteria: Chooses cache-aside for a read-heavy, write-light workload and explains why write-through/read-through is not worth its cost here
Defines TTL as a safety net plus explicit invalidation on writes, with key versioning for whole-class invalidation
Explains the stampede risk and gives a concrete lock-based guard (Cache::lock: one winner recomputes, losers wait and re-read, stale fallback)
Distinguishes penetration, hot-key breakdown, and avalanche and names a mitigation for each
States realistic cases where caching should be avoided and treats Redis as disposable rather than a source of truth
key_points: Cache-aside: read the cache, on miss load from MySQL, store with a TTL; best fit for reads >> writes
Write path: explicit invalidation (Cache::forget or bump products:vN) keeps data fresh; TTL alone is only a fallback
Key versioning lets a single bump invalidate every key of a resource at once
Stampede guard: atomic Cache::lock — only the lock owner recomputes, waiters block and re-read, stale-while-revalidate as last resort
Penetration: cache negative lookups for missing rows or use a bloom filter for absent ids
Breakdown: protect the single hottest key (proactive refresh, never let it expire cold)
Avalanche: jitter TTLs so many keys do not expire simultaneously
Anti-patterns: do not cache secrets, already-cached state, volatile per-request data, or perfectly-fresh-required data; monitor the hit ratio
